title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF BOAZ
paragraphs:
THE UNTOLD STORY OF BOAZ
The Man Everyone Mentions, But Few Truly Know
Most people remember Boaz as the wealthy man who married Ruth.
A supporting character in someone else's story.
But Scripture paints a far deeper portrait.

Behind every field he walked, every handful of grain he dropped, every act of quiet obedience, stood a man carrying scars, memories, and convictions forged through one of the darkest periods in Israel's history.
Boaz was not merely Ruth's redeemer.
Long before he redeemed Ruth, God was redeeming Boaz.
And once you understand his story, you may never read the Book of Ruth the same way again.
Because hidden beneath the surface is a story about broken families, unlikely grace, courageous faith, generational redemption, and a God who specializes in rewriting destinies.
The story begins long before Ruth ever stepped into a barley field.
It begins with a woman many believers overlook.
The Book of Ruth opens with a simple statement:
"In the days when the judges ruled..." (Ruth 1:1)
Those few words carry enormous weight.
The period of the Judges was one of the most spiritually chaotic eras in Israel's history.
The book closes with the haunting refrain:
"Every man did what was right in his own eyes." (Judges 21:25)
Yet into that darkness, God planted a man named Boaz.
The Hebrew name בֹּעַז (Bo'az) likely carries the idea of strength, vigor, or steadfastness.
His name appears again centuries later as one of the pillars of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 7:21), symbolizing strength established by God.
Boaz lived in an age of compromise.
Yet he became a man of conviction.
But his family story makes him unforgettable.
Most readers move past this verse without noticing its implications.
Boaz was the son of Rahab.
The woman everyone expected God to reject.
The woman God chose to save.
The Greek text of Matthew 1:5 reads:
"Σαλμὼν δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Βόες ἐκ τῆς Ῥαχάβ"
"Salmōn de egennēsen ton Boes ek tēs Rachab."
God intentionally preserved her name in the Messiah's genealogy.
Imagine growing up hearing your mother's story.
Imagine knowing that before God's mercy transformed her life, Rahab had lived in a place of shame.
Yet she became living proof that grace is greater than a person's worst chapter.
Boaz did not merely hear about redemption.
His life was evidence that God's mercy can rewrite a family's future.
Perhaps that explains why Boaz recognized something in Ruth that others overlooked.
Because he had seen grace work before.
The Moabites descended from Moab, the son born through the tragic events recorded in Genesis 19.
Relations between Israel and Moab were often hostile.
"No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD..."
Many Israelites viewed Moabites with suspicion.
Ruth carried multiple strikes against her.
Yet Boaz saw something others missed.
The Hebrew word repeatedly emphasized throughout Ruth is חֶסֶד (chesed).
This word is nearly impossible to translate with one English term.
It carries the ideas of covenant love, faithful kindness, steadfast mercy, loyalty, and sacrificial goodness.
And above them all, God demonstrated chesed toward both.
The entire book pulses with this theme.
The kind of love that stays.
The kind of love that sacrifices.
The kind of love that reflects God's own heart.
The first recorded words of Boaz reveal something remarkable.
When he arrives at his fields, he greets his workers:
In the era of the Judges, spiritual integrity was uncommon.
Yet Boaz brought God into everyday life.
His faith was not reserved for worship gatherings.
Everyone around him knew where his allegiance rested.
A great many people talk about faith.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in Scripture.
Not knowing she is walking into divine providence.
As though the narrator is smiling.
Because everyone reading knows it wasn't chance.
God was orchestrating details invisible to human eyes.
Ruth thought she was searching for grain.
God was leading her toward redemption.
And isn't that often how He works?
The person who arrives at precisely the right moment.
What appears random is often divine sovereignty operating behind the curtain.
Boaz could have followed minimum legal requirements.
"Pull out some from the bundles for her and leave it for her to glean." (Ruth 2:16)
Justice required allowing her to glean.
That is the heartbeat of redemption.
Ephesians 3:20 later describes Him as the One who does:
"Exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think."
He becomes a living preview of a greater Redeemer yet to come.
The climax of the story arrives at the city gate.
A nearer kinsman has the first right to redeem Naomi's property.
But when he learns Ruth is included, he withdraws.
The Hebrew concept behind the kinsman-redeemer is גֹּאֵל (go'el).
One who steps into another's loss and assumes responsibility.
But the story points beyond Boaz.
Like Boaz, Jesus entered our brokenness.
Like Boaz, Jesus paid a cost others would not pay.
Like Boaz, Jesus willingly redeemed those unable to redeem themselves.
Like Boaz, Jesus restored what sin had destroyed.
The ending becomes even more astonishing.
Ruth and Boaz have a son named Obed.
A family line marked by outsiders, failures, and unlikely people.
All woven into the genealogy of the Messiah.
Human beings build family trees around achievements.
The genealogy itself becomes a sermon.
Perhaps the untold story of Boaz is not that he was wealthy.
Not even that he redeemed Ruth.
Perhaps the untold story is that Boaz understood grace because he had lived inside its miracle.
He was the son of a redeemed woman.
A living testimony that God specializes in rewriting stories.
That is why he recognized redemption when it stood in his field.
That is why he extended kindness when others withheld it.
That is why he reflected the heart of God.
Because grace received became grace given.
And perhaps that is the challenge hidden within his story.
Many people want the blessing of Boaz.
Few cultivate the character of Boaz.
Yet that is where true transformation begins.
When God's mercy becomes more than something we receive.
Maybe you've spent years believing your past disqualifies you.
Maybe you've spent years feeling like an outsider.
Maybe you've spent years convinced your failures define you.
Because the Gospel has always been a story of God taking what seems ruined and transforming it into something beautiful.
The same God who rewrote Rahab's story.
The same God who rewrote Ruth's story.
The same God who worked through Boaz.
The same God who brought forth King David.
The same God who sent Jesus Christ.
And maybe that is why the story of Boaz continues to move hearts thousands of years later.
Because deep down, every one of us is searching for the same thing.
Someone strong enough to rescue us.
Someone willing enough to pay the cost.
Someone loving enough to call us family.
The people God uses most are often the ones the world least expected Him to keep.
